Chapter 4: Validated Learning—Measuring What Matters
Now that you’ve got your MVP up and running, and you’re working through the Build-Measure-Learn loop, there’s a new challenge ahead: making sure your learning is real—and that it actually drives your business forward.
That’s where validated learning comes in. Think of it as a disciplined way to measure progress, using evidence instead of just gut feelings or wishful thinking.
Validated learning means you’re not just building features or chasing after more users. What really matters is whether those efforts actually lead to meaningful results—like customers sticking around, engaging more, or even spending money.
So, how do you get there? Start by defining clear hypotheses—basically, educated guesses about what you think will make your product successful. Then, put those ideas to the test, just like a scientist would. Run experiments and measure the results using metrics that tell you what’s actually happening.
For instance, imagine your team believes that adding a new feature will get people to use your app more. Instead of just assuming it’ll work, you roll the feature out to a small group. Then, you watch the data closely—does engagement really go up? If not, you’ve learned something valuable, and you can change course before investing more time or money.
Here’s something to watch out for—vanity metrics. These are the numbers that might look great on paper, like total downloads, page views, or how many people follow you on social media. Sure, they feel good, but they don’t always mean your business is making real progress. Sometimes, they just hide the tough problems underneath.
What you really want are actionable metrics—numbers that reveal how your customers behave and whether your business is actually growing. Some of the most useful ones are:
Activation rate: What percentage of users take a key step, like signing up or making a purchase?
Retention rate: How many users keep coming back over time?
Referral rate: Are people telling others about your product?
Revenue per user: On average, how much does each customer spend?
By focusing on these, you’ll see if your experiments are actually moving the needle. Each round through the Build-Measure-Learn loop brings new data, and that data shapes your next decisions.
Validated learning is also your safeguard against falling into what’s called “success theater”—celebrating activity instead of real results. It keeps you honest and focused on what truly counts: building something that people love, and that they’re willing to pay for.
To make all this work, there’s a simple framework you can follow for innovation accounting:
First, establish a baseline—measure how your product does with your earliest users.
Next, tune the engine—keep experimenting and tweaking to improve those key numbers.
And finally, decide whether to pivot or persevere. If you’re seeing strong progress, keep going. If not, it might be time to try a new direction.
When you measure what matters, every action leads to genuine learning and real improvement. Even when things feel uncertain, you’ll have a clear sense of where you’re going—and you’ll make smarter choices about where to invest your team’s precious time and energy.
